short: I'm Dolores Vega from the Eastgate Historical Society. Five people want to lease this building. Take notes, because the clues are in what you hear.

Saint Wenceslas Church was built in 1893 by Czech immigrants. Its cornerstone is still in Czech. The last Czech Mass was in 1971, and Spanish Mass began in 1976. In 1950, four in ten homes spoke Czech. By 2000, seven in ten spoke Spanish. The last Czech business closed in 1994. The Czech heritage society has eleven members, all in the suburbs.

On the side wall, a faded Spanish tortilla sign covers an older Czech beer ad. And what is this place called? Realtors say the Eastgate Arts District. Longtime neighbors say the Barrio. The heritage society says Little Prague.

For ninety-eight years, women ran a sewing and childcare circle in the hall. It closed in 2019. A library survey found seven in ten women avoid this stretch at night because of poor lighting. Income here is about forty-one thousand dollars, rents are up forty percent since 2015, and four in ten homes have no car. Fourteen sidewalk vendors have been cited because they have nowhere legal to sell.
A cultural landscape is the visible mark people leave on a place. Whatever opens here becomes part of it. Let's listen.

Buenos días. I am Rosario Medina. I have owned Panadería La Esperanza on Nineteenth Street since 1982, and I want to build a mercado in the old parish hall. Fourteen vendors, one roof, a legal place to sell. Right now they sell on the sidewalk and the city gives them tickets. Stall rent will be three hundred dollars a month, because that is what they can pay.

A mercado is not only tortillas and chiles you cannot find at the suburban grocery. It is where my nephew got his first job. Where a woman found a room. Where a man found a notary who speaks Spanish. Eleven of the fourteen vendors are family or neighbors from the same towns. That is how people here find work.
When my family came, landlords in other neighborhoods would not rent to us, so we stayed. Now we stay because we want to. It is a cushion against the world. Here, we are home.
Ay, perdón. That is my grandson's ringtone.

I will not make you rich fast. It is cash only, I have no website, and I do not know what return on investment means, exactly. But the stalls will be full on day one, because the vendors are already waiting. Steady money is still money.
Under the Spanish sign on that wall is a Czech one. Every family leaves a line. Let us add one more. Gracias.
Hi, I'm Cole Brennan, and I'm hoppy to be here. Sorry. It's a problem.

I grew up on Nineteenth Street. My mom runs the salon on the corner. I learned to brew in Portland and came home, because the best beer should come from the place that made you. Eastgate Brewing, in the old parish hall. Authentic, local, community. I say "authentic" a lot. My sister counted.

We keep the front of the building, the cornerstone, and we restore the signs on the side wall. First beer: a Czech-style pilsner, because there's a Czech beer ad under that sign. Then Ghost Sign Amber, Cornerstone Stout, Vine and Eighteenth Lager. And no, I won't call anything "the Barrio." That's what my neighbors call home. It's not my brand.
We hire twelve people from within ten blocks. The taproom menu comes from the bakery and tortillería down the street. One wall is reserved for local artists, rent free.

The worry: pints will be eight dollars, which is a lot here, and neighbors told me new places raise prices. I hear that. We'll do a neighbors' night and I'll take feedback monthly. I'm a first-time owner. My brother-in-law made the spreadsheet. Probably fine.
A front porch with a tap handle. Na zdraví.
Maggie Alvarez-Novak, former ER nurse. I have a five-year plan, a ten-year plan, and a plan for if you interrupt me.

The Landing: a women-only gym and co-working floor, plus childcare at six dollars an hour, inside the old parish hall. Forty-five dollars a month. Yes, I'm targeting half the population. That's a larger market than most.

This hall was a women's space for ninety-eight years. My grandmother Anežka sewed in the Wenceslas Women's Circle. My grandmother Lupe sat in the same room when it became the Círculo de Mujeres. In 1921 it was a sewing room because that's what a woman was allowed to be in public. Today it's co-working. Same room, new roles.

The library's night survey: seven in ten women avoid the block by the church after dark. So we build a lit, staffed side entrance on Eighteenth. The nearest licensed daycare is fourteen blocks away. I walked it with a stroller. Twenty-six minutes.
That's not a niche. That's an unmet need with a history. The old Circle room becomes English and Spanish classes, open to everyone.
Slogan: "Sweat. Network. Repeat." Don't workshop it.
I'm not asking nicely. I'm asking accurately. Invest in The Landing.
Brent Hollis-Whitcomb, Hollis and Whitcomb Capital. Let's talk E-Gate. We're branding it SoVine.
I've studied this neighborhood on a real estate app for months. I also did a drive-by on a Sunday. It had a vibe.

The Residences at Vine: sixty luxury lofts. Studios from twenty-four hundred a month. One-bedrooms from thirty-one hundred. Curated ground-floor retail. Think boutique pilates and a fast-casual salad concept. We're not displacing a neighborhood. We're upgrading it.

The old church? A big, empty box and a liability. We've already filed for the demolition permit. But there's a heritage nod: three salvaged bricks in the lobby feature wall, with a plaque. Authentic luxury.
Demand? Rents here are up forty percent in a decade. We pre-tested: ninety percent of units reserved in forty-eight hours, from people who don't live here yet. That's traction.
Existing residents? We're excited to welcome the existing demographic to a more vibrant corner. A rising tide. Community engagement is a flyer with a QR code. It's a good flyer.
I'll skip the community meeting. We close, we demolish, we deliver in eighteen months. Bold. Disruptive. Beautiful. Let's activate the corner.
Na zdraví! Gerry Dvorak, one-eighth Czech, on my mother's side. The best side.

Little Prague Experience: a Bohemian beer hall in the old parish hall. Pretzels the size of your head, strudel, an oompah band every Friday, and I play the accordion. A gift shop with cuckoo clocks, steins, feathered hats, and lederhosen in every size. Is that Czech? It's all basically the same thing. Europe. Central-ish.
Market research: I posted a poll in the Czech heritage society group. Eleven members, nine said yes. That's eighty-two percent. I did the math. I think.

Branding: "Little Prague." That's what the heritage society calls it, so I'm making it official. I'm petitioning to rename the street Little Prague Way. The neighbors will love it. Who doesn't love a pretzel?
The Spanish sign on the side wall? We'll paint a Czech flag over it. It was kind of faded anyway.
Menus in Czech, thanks to my language app streak of eleven days. English on the back. Spanish? We'll see.
Revenue: tourist buses from the suburbs, forty people a bus. Eventually. Everybody loves a theme.
Is it a good investment? It's a great investment in my dream. Which is the same thing. Na zdraví!
